THE SALARY-BASIS REQUIREMENT FOR EXEMPT EMPLOYEES: WHAT COUNTS AS A SALARY AND WHICH DEDUCTIONS ARE RECOGNIZED (LAB. CODE § 515; WAGE ORDER 4-2001, § 1(A); 29 C.F.R. §§ 541.602, 541.603; DLSE ENFORCEMENT MANUAL § 51.6; NEGRI V. KONING & ASSOCIATES; CONLEY V. PACIFIC GAS & ELECTRIC CO.; RHEA V. GENERAL ATOMICS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the salary-basis requirement that accompanies the executive, administrative, and professional overtime exemptions — the requirement that applies to a salaried position such as Operations Manager, held by Jordan Lee. It describes the two-part structure of the exemptions, what a "salary" is (Negri v. Koning & Associates), the federal definition of payment "on a salary basis" that California enforcement follows, the weekly measure of the salary obligation, the recognized deductions for full-day personal absences and for full-day absences covered by a bona fide sickness or disability plan, the rule that no deduction may be made when the employer or the business has no work available, the treatment of partial-day absences and of days on which the employee performs any work, what Conley v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. and Rhea v. General Atomics hold about charging a partial-day absence to an accrued vacation or leave bank, jury duty and military leave, disciplinary suspensions and safety-rule penalties, extra pay for extra work, and what happens to the exemption when an improper deduction is made. It describes the law; it does not classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt, does not evaluate any pay practice, and does not state whether any particular deduction was proper.

THE EXEMPTIONS HAVE A PAY REQUIREMENT IN ADDITION TO A DUTIES REQUIREMENT
California's executive, administrative, and professional overtime exemptions are established by the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders within limits set by Labor Code section 515. Section 515(a) permits those exemptions only where the employee is primarily engaged in exempt duties, customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment, which section 515(c) defines as 40 hours per week. Wage Order 4-2001 states the same pay condition in each of its three exemption definitions. The pay condition has two separate components that are often discussed together but operate independently: the amount of the pay, which is the two-times-minimum-wage threshold, and the form of the pay, which is that the amount must be a salary. This document addresses the second component — what makes pay a salary, and what deductions from it are recognized — and not the threshold amount. The Court of Appeal in Rhea v. General Atomics described the structure as a two-element test under both California and federal law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The Industrial Welfare Commission may establish exemptions from the requirement that an overtime rate of compensation be paid pursuant to Sections 510 and 511 for executive, administrative, and professional employees, if the employee is primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment in performing those duties, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment."
  — California Labor Code section 515 (California Legislative Information), Cal. Lab. Code § 515, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515)
  "Such an employee must also earn a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two (2) times the state minimum wage for full-time employment. Full-time employment is defined in Labor Code Section 515(c) as 40 hours per week."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 1(A)(1)(f) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle4.pdf)
  "Both California and federal law provide that employees are exempt only if they (1) perform certain types of work and (2) are paid on a salary basis."
  — Rhea v. General Atomics (2014) 227 Cal.App.4th 1560, 227 Cal.App.4th 1560, 1567 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2684971/rhea-v-general-atomics/)
  Known gap: The two-times-minimum-wage dollar threshold, the duties tests for each of the three exemptions, and the "primarily engaged in" more-than-half-of-worktime standard are the subject of other documents in this corpus and are not described here. Labor Code section 515 does not itself use the phrase "salary basis" or define "salary," and neither does Wage Order 4-2001; that gap is what led the courts quoted later in this document to federal law. Several occupations are governed by different or additional pay rules not addressed in this document, including computer software employees under Labor Code section 515.5, licensed physicians and surgeons under Labor Code section 515.6, and employees covered by wage orders other than Wage Order 4-2001, whose section 1 text differs in places from the text quoted here.

WHAT MAKES PAY A "SALARY": NEGRI V. KONING & ASSOCIATES
Neither Labor Code section 515 nor Wage Order 4-2001 defines the word "salary." In Negri v. Koning & Associates, the Sixth District Court of Appeal addressed an insurance claims adjuster who was paid $29 per hour with no guaranteed minimum and who received the same $29 per hour no matter how many hours he worked. The court held that a compensation scheme based solely on the number of hours worked, with no guaranteed minimum, is not a salary, so the administrative exemption did not apply regardless of the employee's duties. The court reasoned that the wage order's choice of the specific word "salary," rather than a generic term such as "compensation" or "pay," implies a fixed rate of pay as distinguished from an hourly wage, and that the pay must be something other than an hourly wage. Because the employer stipulated that it never paid a guaranteed salary and that the employee made less money when he worked fewer claims, the pay was not a predetermined amount not subject to reduction based on the quantity of work performed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The question presented in this case is whether a compensation scheme based solely upon the number of hours worked, with no guaranteed minimum, can be considered a “salary” within the meaning of the pertinent wage and hour laws. We conclude that such a payment schedule is not a salary and, therefore, does not qualify the employee as exempt."
  — Negri v. Koning & Associates (2013) 216 Cal.App.4th 392, 216 Cal.App.4th 392, 395 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1037418/negri-v-koning-associates/)
  "Wage Order 4 refers to compensation in the form of a “salary.” It does not define the term. The regulation does not use a more generic term, such as “compensation” or “pay.” Either of these terms would encompass hourly wages, a fixed annual salary, and anything in between. “Salary” is a more specific form of compensation. A salary is generally understood to be a fixed rate of pay as distinguished from an hourly wage."
  — Negri v. Koning & Associates (2013) 216 Cal.App.4th 392, 216 Cal.App.4th 392, 397 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1037418/negri-v-koning-associates/)
  "That is the same thing as saying that plaintiff was not paid “a predetermined amount” that “was not subject to reduction based upon the quantity of work performed.” He was not paid a salary."
  — Negri v. Koning & Associates (2013) 216 Cal.App.4th 392, 216 Cal.App.4th 392, 400 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1037418/negri-v-koning-associates/)
  Known gap: Negri decided only that an hourly compensation scheme with no guaranteed minimum is not a salary; it did not decide how much of a guarantee is enough, and it expressly noted that the employer in fact always paid the equivalent of $29 per hour for 40 hours per week, which the court held did not change the result given the stipulated absence of a guarantee. The opinion arose under the administrative exemption of Wage Order 4-2001 on stipulated facts; this document does not state how the reasoning would apply to an employee paid a fee, a draw against commissions, or a day rate. The quoted sentence beginning "We conclude" appears in the source with the word "salary" set in italics, which the fetched text renders on its own line; that line break has been collapsed to a single space in the quote below.

THE FEDERAL DEFINITION OF PAYMENT "ON A SALARY BASIS" AND ITS USE IN CALIFORNIA
Because the California sources do not define "salary," both the courts and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement look to the federal salary-basis regulation, 29 C.F.R. section 541.602, subject to the rule that California requirements must be at least as protective of the employee as the federal standard. Under that regulation an employee is paid on a salary basis if the employee regularly receives, each pay period on a weekly or less frequent basis, a predetermined amount constituting all or part of the employee's compensation, which amount is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of the work performed. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states the same rule in its Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, adding the California element that the predetermined amount must total at least two times the California minimum wage per month and must be paid on regularly scheduled paydays consistent with California law. The Division also states that it concluded the Industrial Welfare Commission intended enforcement of the salary requirement to follow the federal guidelines so far as possible, but that certain federal guidelines may not be used in California where they conflict with California statutory law, case law, or public policy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "An employee will be considered to be paid on a “salary basis” within the meaning of this part if the employee regularly receives each pay period on a weekly, or less frequent basis, a predetermined amount constituting all or part of the employee's compensation, which amount is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of the work performed."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) (salary basis), 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)
  "The rule is that state law requirements for exemption from overtime pay must be at least as protective of the employee as the corresponding federal standards."
  — Negri v. Koning & Associates (2013) 216 Cal.App.4th 392, 216 Cal.App.4th 392, 398 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1037418/negri-v-koning-associates/)
  "An employee will be considered to be paid “on a salary basis” within the meaning of both the California statute and the IWC Orders, if under his employment agreement he receives on regularly scheduled paydays consistent with California law, a predetermined amount constituting all of part of his compensation, which totals at least two times the California minimum wage per month, which amount is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of the work performed."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 51.6.8 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "In making this determination for purposes of the salary basis test, DLSE has concluded that, to the extent possible, the IWC intended that the enforcement of the “salary” requirement was to follow the federal guidelines so far as possible; but that certain of the federal guidelines may not be utilized in California because they conflict with California statutory law, case law, or public policy."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 51.6.4 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement manual is an agency enforcement document, not a regulation, and its section 51.6 text quoted here carries "JUNE, 2002" and later revision footers; courts treat such agency interpretations as persuasive rather than binding. The sentence quoted from manual section 51.6.8 contains the apparent typographical error "all of part of his compensation" where the federal regulation reads "all or part"; it is quoted as it appears. The manual also cites the pre-2004 federal numbering (29 C.F.R. § 541.118) in places, which the 2004 federal rulemaking replaced with section 541.602; this document quotes the current numbering from the Code of Federal Regulations directly. Which specific federal guidelines the Division regards as incompatible with California law is stated only in the particular manual sections quoted elsewhere in this document.

THE SALARY OBLIGATION IS MEASURED BY THE WEEK
Although Labor Code section 515 and the wage orders state the California salary threshold as a monthly figure, the salary-basis obligation itself is measured week by week. The federal regulation provides that, subject to the listed exceptions, an exempt employee must receive the full salary for any week in which the employee performs any work, without regard to the number of days or hours worked, and that exempt employees need not be paid for any workweek in which they perform no work. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement announced on March 1, 2002 that for enforcement purposes it would follow the federal regulations requiring the salary test to be based on a weekly salary, so that an employer may deduct a week's salary from the monthly salary where the employee performed no work that week, while stating that the monthly salary may not be prorated for part-time employees. The Division's manual states the corresponding affirmative rule: the employee must receive the pro rata share of the full monthly salary for any week in which the employee performs any work, without regard to the number of days or hours worked in the workweek.

  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(1), 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(1) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)

Neither the federal regulation nor the manual passages quoted here state how the weekly measure interacts with an employee whose first or last week of employment is partial; that situation is governed by the separate initial-and-terminal-week provision of 29 C.F.R. section 541.602(b)(6), which is the subject of a different document in this corpus. Nothing in these sources addresses whether an employment contract independently obliges the employer to pay salary for a week in which no work was performed.

DEDUCTIONS FOR ABSENCES OF A FULL DAY OR MORE FOR PERSONAL REASONS
The first recognized exception to the no-deduction rule is an absence of one or more full days for personal reasons other than sickness or disability. The federal regulation gives the example of an employee absent for two full days to handle personal affairs, whose salaried status is not affected by deductions for the two full-day absences, and states that an employee absent for one and a half days for personal reasons may be docked only for the one full-day absence. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement takes the same position, stating that a full-day-or-more absence on personal business may be deducted on a pro rata basis from the salary owed without affecting exempt status. The Division also states the arithmetic it uses for that proration: the predetermined monthly salary is multiplied by 12 to find the yearly salary, that product is divided by 52 to find the weekly salary, and the weekly salary is divided by the usual number of days the employee is scheduled to work in a workweek — with the further limits that the divisor may not be less than five nor more than six, and that no single day of absence may reduce the salary by more than one-fifth.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Deductions from pay may be made when an exempt employee is absent from work for one or more full days for personal reasons, other than sickness or disability. Thus, if an employee is absent for two full days to handle personal affairs, the employee's salaried status will not be affected if deductions are made from the salary for two full-day absences. However, if an exempt employee is absent for one and a half days for personal reasons, the employer can deduct only for the one full-day absence."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(1), 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(1) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)

  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 51.6.14.3 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "Pursuant to that position, DLSE has announced, the proration may be made based upon the number of days in a workweek which the employee usually works; but may not be less than five nor more than six."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 51.6.10 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: The Division's proration formula is an enforcement position drawn from its reading of a July 21, 1997 federal Wage and Hour Division opinion letter, and the manual pages stating it carry a June 2002 footer; the federal regulation itself states in 29 C.F.R. section 541.602(c) only that the employer may use the hourly or daily equivalent of the full weekly salary or any other amount proportional to the time actually missed. The manual's section 51.6.15.1 worked example divides $692.31 by 5 and prints the result as $138.45 in one place and $138.46 in another; neither figure is reproduced as a quotation here. These sources describe when a deduction does not defeat the exemption; they do not address whether a contract, policy, or collective bargaining agreement separately entitles the employee to the deducted amount.

DEDUCTIONS FOR FULL-DAY ABSENCES OCCASIONED BY SICKNESS OR DISABILITY
The second recognized exception covers absences of one or more full days occasioned by sickness or disability, including work-related accidents, where the deduction is made in accordance with a bona fide plan, policy, or practice of providing compensation for loss of salary occasioned by such sickness or disability. Under the federal regulation the employer need not pay any portion of the salary for full-day absences for which the employee receives compensation under the plan, and deductions for such full-day absences may also be made before the employee has qualified under the plan and after the employee has exhausted the leave allowance under it. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states the California version more restrictively in one respect: no deduction may be made for absences occasioned by sickness or accident unless the absence exceeds the weekly period, and deductions in full-working-day increments require a bona fide plan providing full compensation for loss of salary and exhaustion of the employee's leave under the policy. The Division adds that only plans that continue the full amount of the salary of the sick or injured employee are recognized as bona fide, that reasonable probationary periods are permissible, and that state-required disability insurance benefits do not constitute a bona fide sick leave plan.

  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §§ 51.6.16, 51.6.16.1 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)

  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 51.6.16.1 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: The manual's section 51.6.15.2 statement that deductions require exhaustion of leave under the policy is in tension with the federal regulation's statement that deductions may be made both before the employee qualifies under the plan and after the leave allowance is exhausted; the sources are quoted as they read and this document does not reconcile them. The manual passage contains the apparent typographical error "Deductions may by made" and the phrase "increments of full working day," both quoted as they appear. The Division states no definition of "bona fide sickness or disability plans, policies or practices," reporting that the federal regulations contain none and that it will judge each plan case by case. Nothing quoted here addresses California's separate paid sick leave statute or a deduction from an accrued leave bank rather than from salary, which is addressed in a later clause of this document.

NO DEDUCTION WHEN THE EMPLOYER OR THE BUSINESS HAS NO WORK AVAILABLE
The salary-basis definition itself forecloses deductions that follow from the employer's own decisions rather than the employee's absence. The federal regulation states that an employee is not paid on a salary basis if deductions from predetermined compensation are made for absences occasioned by the employer or by the operating requirements of the business, and that if the employee is ready, willing, and able to work, deductions may not be made for time when work is not available. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement adopts the same rule and illustrates it with two examples: an employer who closes the business for three days must pay exempt employees for the full week if they were ready, willing, and able to work but were prevented from doing so by the closure, while an employer who closes for a full week owes no salary for that week provided the employees performed no work at all. The Division notes that this rule, too, is subject to the general principle that no salary need be paid to an exempt employee in a workweek in which no work is performed.

  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(2), 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(2) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)

  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §§ 51.6.14.1, 51.6.14.2 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)

The interaction of these rules with a furlough or a temporary business closure is the subject of a separate document in this corpus. The examples quoted are the Division's own and assume the employee performed no work during the closed week; the effect of any work performed during such a week is described in the following clause.

PARTIAL-DAY ABSENCES AND DAYS ON WHICH THE EMPLOYEE PERFORMS ANY WORK
Because the recognized deductions are framed in full-day units, a deduction from salary for a partial-day absence is not among them. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states the point directly: if an exempt employee performs any work during the work day, no deduction may be made from the salary as a result of what would otherwise be a partial-day absence. The Division also treats work performed away from the employer's premises as work for this purpose, stating that a deduction cannot be made where the employee spends time reviewing files at home, because a deduction is allowed only for an absence of a day or more. The Division extends the same reasoning to time an employee is not genuinely free of duties: if an employer requires an exempt employee on vacation to be available on short notice, expects the employee to call the office or check email, or calls the employee, that is work performed and a reduction in salary would not be appropriate, the salary not being subject to deduction if the employee did not have a reasonable expectation of being free of all duties — though the Division adds that an employee may not unilaterally absent himself and simply announce that he will be available, and that there must be some indication by the employer that the time is not expected to be completely duty-free.

The quoted passages from sections 51.6.12 and 51.6.13 are reproduced exactly as the manual's PDF text renders them, including the stray spaces inside words ("employe e", "tim e", "rev iewin g", "exem pt", "o f", "availab le") and the apparent typographical error "absence of a day of more" where "or more" is evidently meant; those spaces come from the document's own text layer and are not insertions. The quoted passages use masculine pronouns, as the manual does. This clause concerns deductions from salary; whether an employer may instead charge a partial-day absence to an accrued vacation, annual leave, or paid-time-off bank is a separate question addressed in the next clause, where California case law reaches a different result. Whether particular remote work time is itself compensable time worked for other purposes is governed by different rules not addressed here.

CHARGING A PARTIAL-DAY ABSENCE TO AN ACCRUED VACATION OR LEAVE BANK
California case law treats a deduction from an accrued leave bank differently from a deduction from salary. In Conley v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co., employees argued that the employer's policy of charging exempt employees' vacation leave banks for partial-day absences destroyed the salary basis for all of them. The First District Court of Appeal held otherwise, concluding that nothing in California law precludes employers from following the federal rule permitting them to require the use of vacation leave for partial-day absences without causing otherwise exempt employees to become nonexempt. The court reasoned that employees still receive all of the paid time off they have earned and must simply use accrued vacation to make up for partial-day absences, so the policy neither imposes a forfeiture nor prevents vacation pay from vesting; it regulates only the timing of the use of vacation time. The employer's policy in Conley applied only to absences of at least four hours. In Rhea v. General Atomics, the Fourth District Court of Appeal declined to read Conley as establishing a four-hour floor, finding no basis in California law for prohibiting an employer from requiring exempt employees to use vacation or leave time for a partial-day absence and no reason to distinguish among partial-day absences by length.

  "Accordingly, in the published portion of this opinion, we conclude that nothing in California law precludes an employer from following the established federal policy permitting employers to deduct from exempt employees’ vacation leave, when available, on account of partial-day absences from work."
  — Conley v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (2005) 131 Cal.App.4th 260, 131 Cal.App.4th 260, 263 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2281295/conley-v-pacific-gas-electric-co/)
  "In sum, we find nothing in California law that precludes employers from following the federal rule that permits them to require the use of vacation leave for partial-day absences without causing otherwise exempt employees to become nonexempt under the salary basis test."
  — Conley v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (2005) 131 Cal.App.4th 260, 131 Cal.App.4th 260, 271 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2281295/conley-v-pacific-gas-electric-co/)

California's executive, administrative, and professional overtime exemptions are established by the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders within limits set by Labor Code section 515. Section 515(a) permits those exemptions only where the employee is primarily engaged in exempt duties, customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment, which section 515(c) defines as 40 hours per week. Wage Order 4-2001 states the same pay condition in each of its three exemption definitions. The pay condition has two separate components that are often discussed together but operate independently: the amount of the pay, which is the two-times-minimum-wage threshold, and the form of the pay, which is that the amount must be a salary. This document addresses the second component — what makes pay a salary, and what deductions from it are recognized — and not the threshold amount. The Court of Appeal in Rhea v. General Atomics described the structure as a two-element test under both California and federal law.

The federal regulation gives the example of an employee absent for two full days to handle personal affairs, whose salaried status is not affected by deductions for the two full-day absences, and states that an employee absent for one and a half days for personal reasons may be docked only for the one full-day absence. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement takes the same position, stating that a full-day-or-more absence on personal business may be deducted on a pro rata basis from the salary owed without affecting exempt status. The Division also states the arithmetic it uses for that proration: the predetermined monthly salary is multiplied by 12 to find the yearly salary, that product is divided by 52 to find the weekly salary, and the weekly salary is divided by the usual number of days the employee is scheduled to work in a workweek — with the further limits that the divisor may not be less than five nor more than six, and that no single day of absence may reduce the salary by more than one-fifth.

The Division notes that this rule, too, is subject to the general principle that no salary need be paid to an exempt employee in a workweek in which no work is performed.

expectedJSON.body: California case law treats a deduction from an accrued leave bank differently from a deduction from salary. In Conley v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co., employees argued that the employer's policy of charging exempt employees' vacation leave banks for partial-day absences destroyed the salary basis for all of them. The First District Court of Appeal held otherwise, concluding that nothing in California law precludes employers from following the federal rule permitting them to require the use of vacation leave for partial-day absences without causing otherwise exempt employees to become nonexempt. The court reasoned that employees still receive all of the paid time off they have earned and must simply use accrued vacation to make up for partial-day absences, so the policy neither imposes a forfeiture nor prevents vacation pay from vesting; it regulates only the timing of the use of vacation time. The employer's policy in Conley applied only to absences of at least four hours. In Rhea v. General Atomics, the Fourth District Court of Appeal declined to read Conley as establishing a four-hour floor, finding no basis in California law for prohibiting an employer from requiring exempt employees to use vacation or leave time for a partial-day absence and no reason to distinguish among partial-day absences by length.

Rhea has not identified any reason for us to distinguish between partial-day absences of different lengths.

The Division notes that this rule remains subject to the caveat that an employee who performs no work at all during an entire week is not entitled to a continuation of salary for that week, even if the time lost is due to jury duty, witness attendance, temporary military leave, or any other reason.

The federal regulation permits deductions from the pay of exempt employees for penalties imposed in good faith for infractions of safety rules of major significance, describing such rules as those relating to the prevention of serious danger in the workplace or to other employees, and separately permits deductions for unpaid disciplinary suspensions of one or more full days imposed in good faith for infractions of workplace conduct rules, where the suspension is imposed pursuant to a written policy applicable to all employees. The Court of Appeal made the same general observation in Negri v. expectedJSON.body: The consequence of an improper deduction depends on the circumstances. Under the federal regulation an employer who makes improper deductions loses the exemption if the facts demonstrate that the employer did not intend to pay employees on a salary basis, and an actual practice of making improper deductions demonstrates that absence of intent; where such a practice exists, the exemption is lost during the period of the improper deductions for employees in the same job classification working for the same managers responsible for them. Improper deductions that are isolated or inadvertent do not cost the exemption if the employer reimburses the employees. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states a parallel California position: willful deductions in contravention of the salary requirements indicate that there was no intention to pay the employee on a salary basis, so the exemption would not apply and the overtime requirements of the wage orders would apply, while a deduction that is inadvertent or made erroneously but in good faith does not cost the exemption if the employer reimburses the employee on being made aware of the error and agrees in writing to comply in the future. Negri adds that the improper-deduction analysis does not arise at all unless the employer at least attempted to pay the employee on a salary basis.

An actual practice of making improper deductions demonstrates that the employer did not intend to pay employees on a salary basis.

Improper deductions that are either isolated or inadvertent will not result in loss of the exemption for any employees subject to such improper deductions, if the employer reimburses the employees for such improper deductions.

expectedJSON.body: The salary-basis rules govern one question only: whether the pay component of an overtime exemption is satisfied. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states the point expressly, explaining that the requirement of a salary without deduction is simply a criterion that must be met for the employee to be exempt from the overtime requirements of the wage orders, that the remedy for failure to pay a qualifying salary is that the employee is not eligible for the exemption and must be paid premium pay for overtime hours, and that whether an employee has a right to recover salary that was not paid in full is determined by the contract of employment. Satisfying the salary basis does not make a position exempt, because the wage order states the pay condition in addition to the duties tests, and the federal regulation itself provides for situations in which less than a full week's salary may be paid, including the initial or terminal week of employment and weeks in which an exempt employee takes unpaid leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act.
